---
title: "Recovering the EZ diffusion model on the standard grid"
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4,
  out.width = "100%"
)
options(width = 90)
# paths relative to the package root, whether this renders from the
# package root (pkgdown) or from vignettes/articles
from_root <- function(path) {
  if (dir.exists("vignettes")) path else file.path("..", "..", path)
}
# the code shown is read from the script that produced the results
shown <- function(label, file) {
  lines <- readLines(from_root(file))
  markers <- grep("^## ---- ", lines)
  start <- markers[lines[markers] == paste("## ----", label)]
  end <- c(markers[markers > start], length(lines) + 1L)[[1L]] - 1L
  code <- lines[(start + 1L):end]
  while (length(code) > 0L && !nzchar(trimws(code[[length(code)]]))) {
    code <- code[-length(code)]
  }
  code
}
script <- "vignettes/articles/precompute/recovery-ezdm.R"
script_url <- paste0(
  "https://github.com/GidonFrischkorn/bmmtools/blob/main/", script
)
fmt <- function(x, digits = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
# after "at most" or "at least", round outward, so that the printed
# digits still bound the value
fmt_up <- function(x, digits = 2) {
  fmt(ceiling(x * 10^digits - 1e-9) / 10^digits, digits)
}
fmt_down <- function(x, digits = 2) {
  fmt(floor(x * 10^digits + 1e-9) / 10^digits, digits)
}
library(bmmtools)
```

```{r data, include = FALSE}
res <- readRDS(from_root("vignettes/articles/assets/recovery-ezdm.rds"))
out <- res$out
bmm_version <- res$toolchain[["bmm"]]
reps <- length(unique(res$cells$replication))
cells <- res$cells
pop <- res$population
sds <- res$families$sd
subj <- res$families$subject
rel <- res$reliability
rel <- rel[match(
  paste(subj$condition, subj$term), paste(rel$condition, rel$term)
), ]
cors <- res$correlations
readoff <- res$readoff
rows <- as.data.frame(out)
# one row of a table, by design and term; anything but exactly one row is
# an error, so a regenerated asset cannot silently shift the prose
pick <- function(x, n, t, term = NULL) {
  keep <- x$n_subjects == n & x$n_trials == t
  if (!is.null(term)) keep <- keep & x$term == term
  out <- x[keep, ]
  stopifnot(nrow(out) == 1L)
  out
}
smallest <- function(n, threshold, column = "smallest_with_coverage") {
  out <- readoff[readoff$n_subjects == n & readoff$threshold == threshold, ]
  stopifnot(nrow(out) == 1L)
  out[[column]]
}
# the condition label of one design, for the per-design scatter plots
design_of <- function(n, t) {
  d <- res$design[res$design$n_subjects == n & res$design$n_trials == t, ]
  stopifnot(nrow(d) == 1L)
  d$condition
}
# a 95 % Wilson score interval for k of n, as plot_design() draws it
wilson <- function(k, n, z = stats::qnorm(0.975)) {
  p <- k / n
  centre <- (p + z^2 / (2 * n)) / (1 + z^2 / n)
  spread <- z / (1 + z^2 / n) * sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n + z^2 / (4 * n^2))
  c(centre - spread, centre + spread)
}
interval <- function(k, n) paste(fmt(wilson(k, n)), collapse = " to ")
covered <- function(p) paste0(round(p * reps), "/", reps)
with_mcse <- function(x, se) paste0(fmt(x), " ± ", fmt(se, 3))
pars <- res$pars
accuracy <- stats::plogis(pars[["drift"]] * exp(pars[["bound"]]))
mean_rt <- exp(pars[["ndt"]]) + exp(pars[["bound"]]) /
  (2 * pars[["drift"]]) * tanh(pars[["drift"]] * exp(pars[["bound"]]) / 2)
# convergence: which fits fail the gate, and on which parameter the
# lowest bulk ESS of each sits (recorded by the precompute from the fits)
n_pass <- sum(cells$converged)
n_pass_101 <- sum(cells$converged_101)
failing <- cells[!cells$converged, ]
n_fail <- nrow(failing)
n_fail_30 <- sum(failing$n_trials == 30)
fail_on_cor <- sum(grepl("^cor_", failing$min_ess_bulk_parameter))
passing <- cells[cells$converged, ]
pass_on_cor <- sum(grepl("^cor_", passing$min_ess_bulk_parameter))
pass_on_pop <- sum(grepl("^b_", passing$min_ess_bulk_parameter))
# the lowest bulk ESS over all variables, and over all but lp__ and lprior
on_lp <- cells$min_ess_bulk_variable %in% c("lp__", "lprior")
n_fail_bulk <- sum(grepl("ess_bulk", failing$failed))
n_fail_div <- sum(grepl("divergent", failing$failed))
# the verdicts follow the thresholds the text states; tail ESS is not gated
gate_as_stated <- identical(
  grepl("ess_bulk", cells$failed), cells$min_ess_bulk < 400
) && identical(
  grepl("divergent", cells$failed), cells$n_divergent > 10
) && identical(
  grepl("rhat", cells$failed), cells$max_rhat > 1.05
) && !any(grepl("tail", cells$failed))
# the tile figure: share passing per design; the cost figure: mean seconds
pass_share <- tapply(
  cells$converged, list(cells$n_subjects, cells$n_trials), mean
)
secs <- tapply(
  cells$fit_seconds, list(cells$n_subjects, cells$n_trials), mean
)
# the two figures read the cells stored on `out`; they must agree with these
fig_cells <- as.data.frame(attr(out, "cells"))
fig_cells_n <- nrow(fig_cells)
fig_cells <- fig_cells[match(
  paste(cells$condition, cells$replication),
  paste(fig_cells$condition, fig_cells$replication)
), ]
shared_cells <- intersect(names(fig_cells), names(cells))
cells_agree <- fig_cells_n == nrow(cells) &&
  all(c("converged", "failed", "status", "fit_seconds") %in% shared_cells) &&
  all(vapply(shared_cells, function(column) {
    identical(fig_cells[[column]], cells[[column]])
  }, logical(1)))
# coverage pooled over every design, per level and term: does the Wilson
# interval of the 95 % and of the 50 % intervals contain the nominal rate?
pooled <- do.call(rbind, lapply(
  split(rows[rows$level %in% c("population", "sd"), ], ~ level + term,
    drop = TRUE
  ),
  function(d) {
    contains <- function(k, nominal) {
      w <- wilson(k, nrow(d))
      w[[1]] <= nominal && nominal <= w[[2]]
    }
    data.frame(
      level = d$level[[1]], term = d$term[[1]],
      nominal_95 = contains(sum(d$covered), 0.95),
      nominal_50 = contains(sum(d$covered_50), 0.5)
    )
  }
))
pop_ndt <- pooled$level == "population" & pooled$term == "ndt"
pop_rows <- rows[rows$level == "population", ]
ndt_rows <- pop_rows[pop_rows$term == "ndt", ]
ndt_50 <- sum(ndt_rows$covered_50)
ndt_95 <- sum(ndt_rows$covered)
n_pool <- nrow(ndt_rows)
# the pooled figure shows two Wilson intervals per level and term
n_pooled <- 2 * nrow(pooled)
ndt_p <- stats::binom.test(ndt_50, n_pool, 0.5)$p.value
# the most covered 95 % intervals of n_pool at which the Wilson interval
# still excludes 0.95, and how often coverage of 0.90 or 0.85 gives that
k_flag <- max(Filter(function(k) wilson(k, n_pool)[[2]] < 0.95, 0:n_pool))
# population bias: its ±1 MCSE bar, as plot_design() draws it, and the
# share of cells whose bar misses zero when there is no bias (t, 9 df)
pop_true <- tapply(pop_rows$true_value, pop_rows$term, unique)
bias_rel <- max(abs(pop$bias) / abs(pop_true[pop$term]))
bias_se <- sqrt(pmax(pop$rmse^2 - pop$bias^2, 0) / (pop$n - 1))
n_clear <- sum(abs(pop$bias) > bias_se)
p_clear <- 2 * stats::pt(-1, reps - 1)
# the coverage condition: the smallest count that passes, and the chance
# that calibrated intervals pass it, per term and for all three terms
k_pass <- min(Filter(
  function(k) abs(k / reps - 0.95) <= res$coverage_mcse, 0:reps
))
p_pass <- 1 - stats::pbinom(k_pass - 1, reps, 0.95)
n_terms <- length(unique(pop$term))
# 20 against 50 subjects, matched on trials and term
paired <- function(x, column) {
  a <- x[x$n_subjects == 20, ]
  b <- x[x$n_subjects == 50, ]
  b <- b[match(paste(a$n_trials, a$term), paste(b$n_trials, b$term)), ]
  data.frame(
    term = a$term, n_trials = a$n_trials,
    at_20 = a[[column]], at_50 = b[[column]]
  )
}
width <- paired(pop, "ci_width")
rmse <- paired(pop, "rmse")
r_pair <- paired(subj, "r")
# the standard error of each 20 - 50 difference in r: that of each r from
# its interval (Fisher z, symmetric there), taken to r by the delta method
r_lo <- paired(subj, "r_low")
r_hi <- paired(subj, "r_high")
se_r <- function(r, lo, hi) {
  (1 - r^2) * (atanh(hi) - atanh(lo)) / (2 * stats::qnorm(0.975))
}
r_pair$se <- sqrt(
  se_r(r_pair$at_20, r_lo$at_20, r_hi$at_20)^2 +
    se_r(r_pair$at_50, r_lo$at_50, r_hi$at_50)^2
)
r_pair$ratio <- abs(r_pair$at_20 - r_pair$at_50) / r_pair$se
r_se_max <- r_pair[which.max(r_pair$se), ]
# the bound coverage of 50 subjects at 30 and 100 trials, as a count
bound_k <- round(pick(pop, 50, 30, "bound")$coverage * reps)
# population cells at that count or lower, and the chance that calibrated
# intervals give one
p_low <- stats::pbinom(bound_k, reps, 0.95)
n_low <- sum(round(pop$coverage * reps) <= bound_k)
# the SD row with the largest bias, and the SD rows lowest at 300 trials
sd_worst <- sds[which.max(abs(sds$bias)), ]
sd_300 <- sds[sds$n_trials == 300, ]
sd_low <- sd_300[sd_300$coverage == min(sd_300$coverage), ]
sd_low <- sd_low[order(sd_low$term, sd_low$n_subjects), ]
# the SD intervals pooled over terms and subjects, per number of trials, and
# on which side of the truth those that miss at 300 trials lie
sd_rows <- rows[rows$level == "sd", ]
sd_rows$n_trials <- res$design$n_trials[
  match(sd_rows$condition, res$design$condition)
]
sd_k <- tapply(sd_rows$covered, sd_rows$n_trials, sum)
sd_n <- tapply(sd_rows$covered, sd_rows$n_trials, length)
sd_miss_300 <- sd_rows[sd_rows$n_trials == 300 & !sd_rows$covered, ]
n_miss_300 <- nrow(sd_miss_300)
# the chance that all of them miss on the same side, if each side is as
# likely as the other (the two-sided sign test)
sd_sign_p <- stats::binom.test(n_miss_300, n_miss_300, 0.5)$p.value
# the same, counting the fits the misses come from
miss_fits <- table(paste(sd_miss_300$condition, sd_miss_300$replication))
n_fit_300 <- length(miss_fits)
sd_sign_p_fits <- stats::binom.test(n_fit_300, n_fit_300, 0.5)$p.value
# the SDs' bias: its mean per number of trials, its sign from 100 trials
# on, and its size relative to the interval width at 100 and 300 trials
sd_mean_bias <- tapply(sds$bias, sds$n_trials, mean)
sd_100up <- sds[sds$n_trials >= 100, ]
sd_ratio <- function(t) {
  d <- sds[sds$n_trials == t, ]
  d <- d[match(
    paste(sd_300$n_subjects, sd_300$term), paste(d$n_subjects, d$term)
  ), ]
  d$bias / d$ci_width
}
sd_miss_cells <- sd_300$coverage < 1
# contraction: from each fit's link-scale posterior SD and the prior SD
contr_rows <- rows[rows$level %in% c("population", "sd"), ]
contr_prior <- res$prior_sd$prior_sd_link[match(
  paste(contr_rows$level, contr_rows$term),
  paste(res$prior_sd$level, res$prior_sd$term)
)]
contr_link <- isTRUE(all.equal(
  1 - (contr_rows$post_sd_link / contr_prior)^2, contr_rows$contraction
))
contr_min <- min(c(pop$contraction, sds$contraction), na.rm = TRUE)
# ndt's natural scale: its bias, RMSE and width against the largest of the
# three parameters, per row of the population figure
ndt_small <- all(vapply(c("bias", "rmse", "ci_width"), function(column) {
  v <- abs(pop[[column]])
  max(v[pop$term == "ndt"]) < max(v) / 5
}, logical(1)))
# how far the converged-only summary moves r_low
conv_subj <- res$families_converged$subject
r_low_shift <- max(abs(
  conv_subj$r_low[match(
    paste(subj$condition, subj$term),
    paste(conv_subj$condition, conv_subj$term)
  )] - subj$r_low
))
# the generating correlation of 0.4, and the in-sample correlations
cor_rows <- as.data.frame(attr(out, "correlations"))
in_sample <- tapply(
  cor_rows$sample_value, paste(cor_rows$condition, cor_rows$term), mean
)
cors$in_sample <- in_sample[paste(cors$condition, cors$term)]
# the correlation figure summarises the stored correlation rows; the prose,
# its alt text and the table read `cors`. They must agree.
live_cor <- as.data.frame(summary(attr(out, "correlations")))
live_cor_n <- nrow(live_cor)
live_cor <- live_cor[match(
  paste(cors$condition, cors$term), paste(live_cor$condition, live_cor$term)
), ]
cor_columns <- c(
  "rejection_rate", "ci_width", "coverage", "mean_estimate", "bias"
)
cors_agree <- live_cor_n == nrow(cors) && isTRUE(all.equal(
  as.matrix(live_cor[cor_columns]), as.matrix(cors[cor_columns]),
  check.attributes = FALSE
))
target <- cors[cors$true_value == 0.4, ]
readoff <- readoff[order(readoff$n_subjects, readoff$threshold), ]
pair_label <- c(
  bound__drift = "drift – bound", bound__ndt = "bound – ndt",
  drift__ndt = "drift – ndt"
)
# the figures summarise `out` with the installed bmmtools; the tables
# read what the precompute stored. They must agree.
live <- summary(out)
agrees <- function(stored, columns, level) {
  l <- as.data.frame(live)[live$level == level, ]
  same_rows <- nrow(l) == nrow(stored)
  l <- l[match(
    paste(stored$condition, stored$term), paste(l$condition, l$term)
  ), ]
  same_rows && isTRUE(all.equal(
    as.matrix(l[columns]), as.matrix(stored[columns]),
    check.attributes = FALSE
  ))
}
# the read-off by hand, and as smallest_design() gives it: the largest
# answer over the terms, per number of subjects
by_package <- function(threshold, coverage_check) {
  d <- smallest_design(
    live[live$level %in% c("subject", "population"), ],
    c(r_low = threshold),
    coverage_check = coverage_check
  )
  vapply(split(d$smallest, d$n_subjects), function(v) {
    if (anyNA(v)) NA_real_ else max(v)
  }, numeric(1))
}
same_answer <- function(column, coverage_check) {
  all(vapply(c(0.7, 0.8, 0.9), function(t) {
    hand <- readoff[readoff$threshold == t, ]
    pkg <- by_package(t, coverage_check)[as.character(hand$n_subjects)]
    identical(unname(pkg), as.numeric(hand[[column]]))
  }, logical(1)))
}
# drift's r_low answer is larger than bound's and ndt's, at every threshold
# and number of subjects ("not reached" counting as larger than any)
drift_decides <- all(vapply(c(0.7, 0.8, 0.9), function(t) {
  d <- smallest_design(
    live[live$level %in% c("subject", "population"), ], c(r_low = t),
    coverage_check = FALSE
  )
  a <- ifelse(is.na(d$smallest), Inf, d$smallest)
  all(vapply(split(seq_len(nrow(d)), d$n_subjects), function(i) {
    a[i][d$term[i] == "drift"] > max(a[i][d$term[i] != "drift"])
  }, logical(1)))
}, logical(1)))
# drift has the lowest r and model reliability at every design
drift_lowest <- all(vapply(split(seq_len(nrow(subj)), subj$condition),
  function(i) {
    is_drift <- subj$term[i] == "drift"
    r <- subj$r[i]
    m <- rel$reliability_model[i]
    r[is_drift] < min(r[!is_drift]) && m[is_drift] < min(m[!is_drift])
  }, logical(1)
))
# the model's reliability against the truth's, from 100 trials on
gap_100_20 <- rel$reliability_gap[rel$n_trials >= 100 & rel$n_subjects == 20]
gap_100_50 <- rel$reliability_gap[rel$n_trials >= 100 & rel$n_subjects == 50]
gap_30 <- rel$reliability_gap[rel$n_trials == 30]
# the correlation figure: the share excluding zero of the pairs at 0
null_max <- max(cors$rejection_rate[cors$true_value == 0])
target_max_50 <- max(target$rejection_rate[target$n_subjects == 50])
miss_k <- round((1 - target_max_50) * reps)
# the largest 20 - 50 difference in r
r_big <- r_pair[which.max(abs(r_pair$at_20 - r_pair$at_50)), ]
# the small scatter figure, on its own rows: the mean CrI width over the SD
# of the generating values, per parameter
first_small <- out$level == "subject" & out$replication == 1 &
  out$condition == design_of(20, 30)
small <- as.data.frame(out[first_small, ])
small_width <- tapply(small$ci_high - small$ci_low, small$term, mean) /
  tapply(small$true_value, small$term, stats::sd)
# drift's population posterior SD, which has no contraction
drift_post_sd <- pop_rows$post_sd_link[pop_rows$term == "drift"]
# the prose below states these; a regenerated asset must still satisfy them
stopifnot(
  reps == 10,
  smallest(50, 0.8) == 300, smallest(50, 0.7) == 300,
  smallest(50, 0.7, "smallest") == 100, smallest(20, 0.7) == 100,
  is.na(smallest(50, 0.9)), smallest(20, 0.8) == 300,
  smallest(20, 0.8, "smallest_point") == 100,
  same_answer("smallest_with_coverage", TRUE),
  same_answer("smallest", FALSE),
  pick(pop, 50, 30, "bound")$coverage == 0.8,
  pick(pop, 50, 100, "bound")$coverage == 0.8,
  pick(pop, 50, 300, "bound")$coverage == 0.9,
  !pick(pop, 50, 100, "bound")$coverage_ok,
  all(pop$coverage_ok[pop$n_trials == 300]),
  all(abs(pop$bias) < 0.05),
  drift_lowest,
  pick(subj, 50, 100, "drift")$r_low < 0.8,
  pick(subj, 50, 300, "drift")$r_low >= 0.8,
  all(cells$status == "ok"),
  all(target$coverage >= 0.9),
  n_fail_30 > n_fail / 2, fail_on_cor > n_fail / 2,
  all(grepl("^(cor|sd)_", failing$min_ess_bulk_parameter)),
  ndt_95 == nrow(ndt_rows), !pooled$nominal_50[pop_ndt],
  all(pooled$nominal_95), all(pooled$nominal_50[!pop_ndt]),
  ndt_50 / n_pool > 0.5, ndt_p < 0.05 / n_pooled,
  wilson(n_pool, n_pool)[[1]] < 0.95,
  all(width$at_20 > width$at_50),
  all(rmse$at_20[rmse$term == "drift"] > rmse$at_50[rmse$term == "drift"]),
  max(abs(r_pair$at_20 - r_pair$at_50)) < 0.05,
  pick(pop, 50, 100, "bound")$coverage * reps == bound_k,
  wilson(bound_k, reps)[[2]] < 0.95, wilson(bound_k, reps)[[2]] > 0.9,
  sd_worst$term == "drift", all(abs(subj$coverage - 0.95) < 0.05),
  pick(target, 50, 300)$rejection_rate ==
    max(target$rejection_rate[target$n_subjects == 50]),
  pick(target, 20, 300)$rejection_rate ==
    max(target$rejection_rate[target$n_subjects == 20]),
  # drift's r at 50 x 300 meets 0.90 only in the sixth decimal, as printed
  pick(subj, 50, 300, "drift")$r >= 0.900001,
  pick(subj, 50, 300, "drift")$r < 0.90001,
  grepl("^0\\.90000[1-9]$", fmt(pick(subj, 50, 300, "drift")$r, 6)),
  pick(subj, 50, 300, "drift")$r_low < 0.9,
  # the population and SD scales the text names
  all(rows$scale[rows$level %in% c("population", "subject")] == "natural"),
  all(rows$scale[rows$level == "sd"] == "link"),
  all(live$scale[live$level %in% c("population", "subject")] == "natural"),
  all(live$scale[live$level == "sd"] == "link"),
  # the gate and the convergence and cost figures
  gate_as_stated, pass_on_cor > n_pass / 2,
  # the gate's lowest bulk ESS lands on lp__ or lprior in some fits; the
  # counts in the text leave those two out and are otherwise the same
  any(on_lp),
  !any(cells$min_ess_bulk_parameter %in% c("lp__", "lprior")),
  identical(
    cells$min_ess_bulk_parameter[!on_lp], cells$min_ess_bulk_variable[!on_lp]
  ),
  cells_agree,
  max(pass_share[, "30"]) < min(pass_share[, colnames(pass_share) != "30"]),
  all(apply(secs, 1, diff) > 0), all(secs["50", ] > secs["20", ]),
  # bias and coverage of the population means
  all(pop$n == reps),
  stats::pbinom(n_clear - 1, nrow(pop), p_clear, lower.tail = FALSE) > 0.05,
  stats::pbinom(n_low - 1, nrow(pop), p_low, lower.tail = FALSE) > 0.05,
  k_pass == 9,
  identical(pop$coverage_ok, abs(pop$coverage - 0.95) <= res$coverage_mcse),
  round(min(sd_300$coverage) * reps) == bound_k,
  # contraction on the link scale; none for drift's population mean, whose
  # Cauchy prior has no SD, and a value for every other row
  contr_link,
  all(is.na(pop$contraction[pop$term == "drift"])),
  !anyNA(pop$contraction[pop$term != "drift"]), !anyNA(sds$contraction),
  !any(res$prior_sd$term[res$prior_sd$level == "population"] == "drift"),
  length(drift_post_sd) == nrow(cells), !anyNA(drift_post_sd),
  ndt_small,
  # the SDs at 300 trials: fewer covered than at 30 and at 100, which tie;
  # every miss above the truth, two of them from one fit
  sd_n[["30"]] == sd_n[["300"]], sd_n[["100"]] == sd_n[["300"]],
  sd_k[["30"]] == sd_k[["100"]], sd_k[["300"]] < sd_k[["30"]],
  n_miss_300 > 0, all(sd_miss_300$ci_low > sd_miss_300$true_value),
  max(miss_fits) == 2, sum(miss_fits == 2) == 1,
  # a small positive bias, zero or above in every cell from 100 trials on,
  # and larger relative to the width at 300 than at 100 where 300 misses
  all(sd_mean_bias > 0), all(sd_100up$bias >= 0),
  nrow(sd_300) == 6, any(sd_miss_cells),
  all((sd_ratio(300) > sd_ratio(100))[sd_miss_cells]),
  # one more covered bound interval at 50 x 100 would pass the condition,
  # and drift and ndt pass it there already
  abs((bound_k + 1) / reps - 0.95) <= res$coverage_mcse,
  pick(pop, 50, 100, "drift")$coverage_ok,
  pick(pop, 50, 100, "ndt")$coverage_ok,
  # subject parameters and the read-off
  drift_decides,
  # 20 against 50 subjects: the largest standard error of the difference in
  # r is drift's at 30 trials
  r_se_max$term == "drift", r_se_max$n_trials == 30,
  max(r_pair$ratio) < stats::qnorm(0.975),
  r_big$at_20 > r_big$at_50,
  # with 20 subjects the model's reliability is nowhere above the truth's
  # by more than 0.001 from 100 trials on
  max(gap_100_20) <= 0.001,
  # drift's r at 50 x 300 is the 300 under "using r" at 0.90
  smallest(50, 0.9, "smallest_point") == 300,
  # the small scatter figure: drift's intervals the widest relative to the
  # spread of the generating values
  small_width[["drift"]] > max(small_width[names(small_width) != "drift"]),
  identical(
    vapply(c(0.7, 0.8, 0.9), function(t) smallest(20, t, "smallest"), 1),
    vapply(c(0.7, 0.8, 0.9), function(t) smallest(50, t, "smallest"), 1)
  ),
  # the correlation of 0.4: missed at 50 x 300, pulled towards zero at 20 x 30
  miss_k > 0, null_max < target_max_50,
  pick(target, 20, 30)$mean_estimate > 0,
  pick(target, 20, 30)$mean_estimate < pick(target, 20, 30)$in_sample,
  agrees(pop, c("bias", "rmse", "coverage", "ci_width"), "population"),
  agrees(sds, c("bias", "rmse", "coverage", "ci_width"), "sd"),
  agrees(subj, c("r", "r_low", "r_high"), "subject"),
  agrees(rel, "reliability_model", "subject"),
  cors_agree
)
```

This page reports one parameter recovery study of the three-parameter
EZ diffusion model, `bmm::ezdm()`, fitted with bmm `r bmm_version`. The
model describes each person's accuracy and response times by a drift
rate (`drift`), a boundary separation (`bound`) and a non-decision time
(`ndt`), estimated in one Bayesian hierarchical model. Data were
simulated from known parameter values, the model was fitted to
them, and the estimates were compared with the values that generated
the data. A researcher planning an EZ diffusion study can read from it
how well each parameter is recovered with 20 or 50 subjects and 30, 100
or 300 trials per subject, and how many trials per person an analysis of
individual differences needs at the generating values used here. It does
not say how many subjects a study
of group means or of correlations between parameters needs; it shows
only what 20 and 50 subjects give.

A *design* is one combination of subjects and trials; the grid has six.
Each design was simulated and fitted `r reps` times, the
*replications*, so the study has `r nrow(cells)` fits. The page reads
every number from the stored results of those fits, so the page builds
without refitting anything. bmmtools plans a *validation card* for each
model it supports, a standard report on the same grid of designs; the
card for `ezdm` will replace this page
([issue #21](https://github.com/GidonFrischkorn/bmmtools/issues/21)).

**Reading the figures.** Most figures below are drawn by
`plot_design()`: a quantity on the y axis, the number of trials on a log
x axis, one line for 20 and one for 50 subjects, and one panel per
parameter. Each row of panels has its own y axis, shared by the panels
in it. A point is the mean over a
design's ten replications, and its bar shows how precisely ten
replications pin that mean down. For bias and interval width the bar is
±1 *Monte Carlo standard error* (MCSE), the SD over the replications
divided by √10; for RMSE it is ±1 MCSE of the mean squared error,
divided by twice the RMSE (the delta method). For coverage and other
shares the bar is a 95 % *Wilson interval*: the range of true shares
that the observed count is consistent with. It stays between 0 and 1 and is not empty at 10 of
10: ten covered intervals out of ten are consistent with a true coverage
as low as `r fmt_up(wilson(10, 10)[[1]], 3)`, the lower end of the bar. A
dashed line marks the target where there is one: zero for bias, the
nominal 0.95 for coverage. The help page of `plot_design()` states the
source of every bar. The numbers behind each figure are in a table under
it, folded away; the text does not need them.

## The model and the generating values

The values below are on each parameter's link scale, explained after
the code.

```{r model, eval = FALSE, code = shown("model", script)}
```

Each parameter is estimated on its *link scale*, the unbounded scale
the model works on: `drift` as it is, `bound` and `ndt` as logarithms,
so a between-subject SD of 0.2 on `ndt` means people differ by about
20 % in non-decision time. The three-parameter EZ model fixes `s`, the
within-trial noise of the diffusion process, to 1. At these population
values a person answers correctly on `r fmt(100 * accuracy, 1)` % of
trials, with a mean response time of `r fmt(mean_rt, 2)` s (the
EZ expressions for accuracy and mean response time with `s = 1`).
`prior_sd` holds the prior SD of each parameter under bmm's default
priors; it is used for the *contraction* reported in the tables.

## The run

```{r run, eval = FALSE, code = shown("run", script)}
```

`reps = 10` is the number of replications per design. bmmtools
`r res$run_info$bmmtools_version`, which ran the script, did not pass
`seed` on to the chains' starting values, so a second run gave estimates
that differ in the third decimal; later versions seed them too. The one
place where that matters is said below.

<details>
<summary>What the other arguments do</summary>

`re_cor = "all"` lets the model estimate all three between-subject
correlations. `levels` and `correlations = "model"` choose what is
compared with the truth: the population means, the between-subject SDs,
every subject's parameters, and the model's correlation estimates.
`seed` fixes the simulated data and the sampler's seed. The arguments
after it go to `bmm::bmm()`: four chains of 2000 iterations each, the
first 1000 of them warm-up. The help page of `recovery_grid()` explains
the rest.

</details>

```{r convergence-tile, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 3.4, fig.alt = "Six tiles, one per design, with rows for 20 and 50 subjects and columns for 30, 100 and 300 trials. Each tile shows how many of its ten fits pass the convergence gate and which checks the others fail; the tiles at 30 trials are the lightest."}
plot_design(out, type = "convergence")
```

Every fit goes through bmmtools' convergence gate, which asks whether
the sampler explored the posterior well enough to trust the fit. A tile
counts the fits that fail each check, and one fit can fail more than
one.

<details>
<summary>What the gate checks</summary>

The gate checks every parameter of the fit, the between-subject
correlations and each person's values included, and also `lp__` and
`lprior`, the log posterior and the log prior. *R-hat* compares the
chains and should be close to 1; the gate allows at most 1.05. The
*effective sample size* (ESS) counts how many independent draws the
chains are worth; the gate asks for at least 400 in the bulk of the
posterior. The ESS in its tails is reported, not gated. *Divergent
transitions* are steps where the sampler failed; the gate allows at
most 10.

</details>

`r n_pass` of the `r nrow(cells)` fits pass; `r n_pass_101` pass if
R-hat must also be at most 1.01. Of the `r n_fail` fits that fail,
`r n_fail_30` are at 30 trials; `r n_fail_bulk` fail on bulk ESS and
`r n_fail_div` on divergences. Leaving out `lp__` and `lprior`, the
lowest bulk ESS sits on a between-subject correlation in most fits,
failing or not (`r fail_on_cor` of `r n_fail`, and `r pass_on_cor` of
the `r n_pass` that pass), and on a population mean in none that fails
and in `r pass_on_pop` of those that pass.
The results below use every fit; using only those that pass changes no
`r_low` value (the lower end of the interval of r, defined with the
subject parameters) by more than `r fmt_up(r_low_shift, 3)`.

```{r cost, fig.width = 5, fig.height = 2.8, fig.alt = "Seconds per fit against the number of trials, one line for 20 and one for 50 subjects; both rise with trials, and 50 subjects take longer at every number of trials."}
plot_design(out, metric = "fit_seconds")
```

A point is the mean seconds per fit of a design. Fitting took
`r fmt(res$minutes_fitting, 1)` minutes in all (bmm `r bmm_version`,
CmdStan `r res$toolchain[["cmdstan"]]`), between
`r fmt_down(min(cells$fit_seconds), 1)` and
`r fmt_up(max(cells$fit_seconds), 1)` seconds per fit.

<details>
<summary>The convergence numbers per design</summary>

```{r convergence-table, echo = FALSE}
by_design <- split(cells, ~ n_subjects + n_trials)
tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(by_design, function(d) {
  data.frame(
    subjects = d$n_subjects[[1]], trials = d$n_trials[[1]],
    `fits passing the gate` = sum(d$converged),
    `passing with R-hat ≤ 1.01` = sum(d$converged_101),
    `fits with any divergence (the gate allows 10)` =
      sum(d$n_divergent > 0),
    `mean seconds per fit` = fmt(mean(d$fit_seconds), 1),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}))
knitr::kable(
  tab[order(tab$subjects, tab$trials), ],
  row.names = FALSE, align = "r"
)
```

</details>

## Population means

```{r population, fig.height = 6.5, fig.alt = "Bias, RMSE, coverage and credible interval width of the population means of drift, bound and ndt, on the natural scale (seconds for ndt), against the number of trials, one line for 20 and one for 50 subjects."}
plot_design(out)
```

For each fit the estimate is the posterior median. *Bias* is the mean,
over the ten replications, of estimate minus generating value; *RMSE* is
the root of the mean squared difference; *CrI width* is the mean width
of the 95 % credible interval (CrI); all three are on the natural
scale, seconds for `ndt`. Because `ndt` is in seconds, its panels in
these three rows look flat on the y axis each row shares; do not compare
them with drift's by height.
*Coverage* is the share of the replications whose 95 % CrI contains the
generating value. Intervals of the right width contain it 95 % of the
time; intervals that contain it less often are too narrow, and ones that
contain it more often are too wide. For a Bayesian interval at fixed
generating values this holds only approximately (exactly only on average
over the prior); the approximation is close here because the data
outweigh the prior,
with a mean contraction of at least `r fmt_down(contr_min, 2)` in the
tables below and, for drift's population mean, which has none, a
posterior SD of at most `r fmt_up(max(drift_post_sd), 2)` against the
Cauchy prior's scale of 1.

The population means show no bias of practical size: at most
`r fmt_up(max(abs(pop$bias)), 3)` in absolute value, and at most
`r fmt_up(100 * bias_rel, 1)` % of the generating value. In
`r n_clear` of the `r nrow(pop)` cells the ±1 MCSE bar misses zero;
with no bias at all, `r fmt(nrow(pop) * p_clear, 1)` would on average
if the estimates are normal around the truth.
More subjects narrow
the intervals at every design and, for drift, lower the RMSE. Coverage
is where ten replications show their limit. The CrI of `bound` covered
in `r bound_k` of `r reps` replications with 50 subjects at both 30 and
100 trials. The Wilson interval of `r bound_k` of `r reps` runs from
`r interval(bound_k, reps)`, ending just below 0.95. Across the
`r nrow(pop)` cells that is no more than chance gives: intervals of the
right width cover in `r bound_k` or fewer of `r reps` with probability
`r fmt(p_low, 3)`, so `r fmt(nrow(pop) * p_low, 2)` of the
`r nrow(pop)` cells are expected to cover that rarely, and this run has
`r n_low`. Pooled over all six
designs, `bound`'s intervals cover at a rate whose interval contains
0.95 (the pooled coverage figure below).

```{r pooled, fig.height = 3.4, fig.alt = "Coverage of the 50 % and 95 % intervals of each parameter, pooled over all designs, for population means and between-subject SDs, with 95 % Wilson intervals and a dashed line at the nominal rate. Every Wilson interval contains its nominal rate except that of the 50 % intervals of population ndt, which cover more often."}
plot_design(out, type = "coverage")
```

This figure pools the six designs, so each parameter has `r n_pool`
intervals, on the assumption that all six share one coverage. Besides
the 95 % interval, every fit also reported a 50 % interval, a second
check of the width: it should contain the truth half of the time.
Population means are in the upper row, between-subject SDs in the
lower. For the 95 % intervals, `r n_pool` are still few: their Wilson
interval excludes 0.95 only at `r k_flag` or fewer covered, which a
true coverage of 0.90 gives with probability
`r fmt(stats::pbinom(k_flag, n_pool, 0.9))` and one of 0.85 with
`r fmt(stats::pbinom(k_flag, n_pool, 0.85))`. Even at `r n_pool` of
`r n_pool` it reaches down to `r fmt_up(wilson(n_pool, n_pool)[[1]], 3)`,
so it cannot show intervals that are too wide.

Every pooled Wilson interval contains its nominal value but one:
population `ndt`'s 50 % intervals cover in `r ndt_50` of `r n_pool`
(Wilson interval `r interval(ndt_50, n_pool)`, which excludes 0.50).
With `r n_pooled` intervals in the figure, one such miss is no surprise:
if each missed by chance one time in 20, independently, at least one
would with probability `r fmt(1 - 0.95^n_pooled)`. But the exact
binomial p-value of `r ndt_50` of `r n_pool` at 0.50 is
`r fmt(ndt_p, 4)`, below 0.05 / `r n_pooled` =
`r fmt(0.05 / n_pooled, 4)`. The 95 % intervals of population `ndt`
cover in all `r ndt_95`; they come from the same posteriors, so they are
not a second finding. Its 50 % intervals are wider than their nominal
mass.
This run is the only evidence for it so far: the second run mentioned
above used the same simulated data, so it cannot confirm it.

<details>
<summary>The population numbers per design</summary>

*Contraction* is 1 − (posterior SD / prior SD)², both on the link scale,
unlike the other columns: near 1 when the data determine the estimate
and near 0 when the posterior is still the prior.
Averaged over the replications, as in the table, it is at least
`r fmt_down(min(pop$contraction, na.rm = TRUE), 3)` for `bound` and
`ndt`: a posterior variance, on average, at most
`r fmt_up(100 * (1 - min(pop$contraction, na.rm = TRUE)), 1)` % of the
prior variance. `drift` has none, because its
default prior on the population value is a Cauchy distribution, which
has no SD.

```{r population-table, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  subjects = pop$n_subjects, trials = pop$n_trials, parameter = pop$term,
  bias = fmt(pop$bias, 3), RMSE = fmt(pop$rmse, 3),
  covered = covered(pop$coverage),
  `CrI width` = fmt(pop$ci_width, 3),
  contraction = ifelse(
    is.na(pop$contraction), "–", fmt(pop$contraction, 3)
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
), row.names = FALSE, align = "r")
```

</details>

## Between-subject SDs

```{r sd, fig.height = 6.5, fig.alt = "Bias, RMSE, coverage and credible interval width of the between-subject SDs of drift, bound and ndt, on the link scale, against the number of trials, one line for 20 and one for 50 subjects."}
plot_design(out, level = "sd")
```

The SDs are read the same way, but on the link scale. Their bias is at
most `r fmt_up(max(abs(sds$bias)), 3)`, for `r sd_worst$term` at
`r sd_worst$n_subjects` subjects and `r sd_worst$n_trials` trials. Their
coverage drops to `r covered(min(sd_300$coverage))` at 300 trials
(`r paste0(sd_low$term, " with ", sd_low$n_subjects, " subjects", collapse = ", ")`),
with the same wide Wilson interval as above; pooled over the designs,
every SD's interval contains the nominal rate (the figure above). Over
the three SDs and both numbers of subjects, `r sd_k[["300"]]` of
`r sd_n[["300"]]` intervals cover at 300 trials, against
`r sd_k[["30"]]` at 30 and at 100, and all `r n_miss_300` that miss at
300 lie above the truth, their lower ends by at most
`r fmt_up(max(sd_miss_300$ci_low - sd_miss_300$true_value), 3)`. If
misses fell above and below equally often, all `r n_miss_300` would fall
on one side with probability `r fmt(sd_sign_p, 4)`. That treats the
misses as independent, but two of them come from one fit; counting the
`r n_fit_300` fits instead gives 2 × 0.5^`r n_fit_300`^ =
`r fmt(sd_sign_p_fits, 3)`. This was found by looking at the results,
not tested in advance. It fits a small positive bias: the mean bias of
the SDs is `r fmt(sd_mean_bias[["30"]], 3)`,
`r fmt(sd_mean_bias[["100"]], 3)` and `r fmt(sd_mean_bias[["300"]], 3)`
at 30, 100 and 300 trials, and zero or above in all
`r nrow(sd_100up)` cells from 100 trials on. Relative to the interval
width, the bias is larger at 300 trials than at 100 in all
`r sum(sd_miss_cells)` cells with a miss at 300. Ten replications cannot
settle this, and the pooled figure, which assumes one coverage for all
six designs, cannot show it.

<details>
<summary>The SD numbers per design</summary>

```{r sd-table, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  subjects = sds$n_subjects, trials = sds$n_trials, parameter = sds$term,
  bias = fmt(sds$bias, 3), RMSE = fmt(sds$rmse, 3),
  covered = covered(sds$coverage), `CrI width` = fmt(sds$ci_width, 3),
  contraction = fmt(sds$contraction, 3),
  check.names = FALSE
), row.names = FALSE, align = "r")
```

</details>

## Subject parameters

```{r subject, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "r, model-based reliability and coverage of the subject parameters of drift, bound and ndt, against the number of trials, one line for 20 and one for 50 subjects. drift has the lowest r and reliability at every design."}
plot_design(out, level = "subject")
```

Here each person's estimate is compared with that person's generating
value. The question is how well a study of this size ranks people, which
is what an analysis of individual differences needs.

- *r* is, within one replication, the correlation between estimated and
  generating values across the people. The ten values of r are averaged
  after Fisher's z transformation. Its bar runs from *r_low* to
  *r_high*, the usual 95 % interval of that average,
  `tanh(z ± 1.96 / sqrt(N))` with `N` the sum of (people − 3) over the
  replications. r_low is the value the section "How many trials?" uses,
  because it is r with the uncertainty of ten replications taken off.
- *Reliability (model)* answers the same question without the truth, so
  a study can compute it on its own data: `var(m) / (var(m) + mean(v))`,
  with `m` the posterior means of the people and `v` their posterior
  variances, per replication and then averaged.
- *Coverage* is the share of all people's 95 % CrIs that contain their
  generating value. It stays within
  `r fmt_up(max(abs(subj$coverage - 0.95)), 3)` of 0.95 at every design.

`bound` and `ndt` are recovered well from 30 trials on
(r ≥ `r fmt_down(min(subj$r[subj$term != "drift"]))`). `drift` is the hard
parameter: with 50 subjects its r is
`r fmt(pick(subj, 50, 30, "drift")$r)` at 30 trials,
`r fmt(pick(subj, 50, 100, "drift")$r)` at 100 and
`r fmt(pick(subj, 50, 300, "drift")$r)` at 300. More people do not make
each person's estimate detectably better: r is higher with 20 subjects
than with 50 in `r sum(r_pair$at_20 > r_pair$at_50)` of the
`r nrow(r_pair)` comparisons at equal trials, the largest difference
included, and at no design does r differ by more than `r fmt_up(max(abs(r_pair$at_20 - r_pair$at_50)), 3)` between
20 and 50 subjects, or by more than
`r fmt_up(max(r_pair$ratio), 1)` standard errors of the difference. Ten
replications would miss a true gain of less than 1.96 such standard
errors more often than they would detect it, and that standard error is
up to `r fmt_up(r_se_max$se, 3)`, for drift at 30 trials. From 100
trials on, with 20 subjects, the reliability from the model is nowhere
above the squared correlation with the truth (in the table below) by
more than 0.001, and below it by at most
`r fmt_up(max(-gap_100_20), 3)`; with 50 it differs from it by at most
`r fmt_up(max(abs(gap_100_50)), 3)`. At 30 trials the
gap reaches `r fmt(max(abs(gap_30)), 3)`. So on data of that size
from this model, it says how well the people are ranked, a little
pessimistically with 20 subjects.

The two figures below show the first replication of the smallest and of
the largest design: each person's estimate against their generating
value, on the natural scale (seconds for `ndt`), with the 95 % CrI. The
dashed line is where estimate and truth are equal. These panels are in
alphabetical order.

```{r scatter-small, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 2.8, fig.alt = "Estimated against generating subject values for bound, drift and ndt with 20 subjects and 30 trials, one replication; relative to the spread of the generating values, the intervals are widest for drift."}
first <- out$level == "subject" & out$replication == 1
plot_recovery(out[first & out$condition == design_of(20, 30), ])
```

```{r scatter-large, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 2.8, fig.alt = "Estimated against generating subject values for bound, drift and ndt with 50 subjects and 300 trials, one replication; the points lie close to the diagonal with narrow intervals."}
first <- out$level == "subject" & out$replication == 1
plot_recovery(out[first & out$condition == design_of(50, 300), ])
```

<details>
<summary>The subject numbers per design</summary>

*Reliability from the truth* is the squared correlation of `m` with the
generating values; *gap* is the model's reliability minus it, per
replication, then averaged. Each is given with its MCSE, the SD over
replications divided by √10.

```{r subject-table, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  subjects = subj$n_subjects, trials = subj$n_trials, parameter = subj$term,
  r = fmt(subj$r), r_low = fmt(subj$r_low),
  `reliability from the truth` =
    with_mcse(rel$reliability_true, rel$reliability_true_mcse),
  `reliability from the model` =
    with_mcse(rel$reliability_model, rel$reliability_model_mcse),
  gap = with_mcse(rel$reliability_gap, rel$reliability_gap_mcse),
  check.names = FALSE
), row.names = FALSE, align = "r")
```

</details>

## The correlation between drift and boundary

```{r correlation, fig.height = 6.5, fig.alt = paste0("Bias, coverage, credible interval width and the share of intervals excluding zero for the three between-subject correlations, against the number of trials, one line for 20 and one for 50 subjects. The two pairs generated at 0 have a share excluding zero of at most ", fmt_up(null_max, 1), " at every design; the drift-bound pair, generated at 0.4, reaches ", fmt(max(target$rejection_rate), 1), ".")}
plot_design(out, level = "correlation")
```

The simulation drew each person's drift rate and boundary separation
from a population in which they correlate 0.4 and left the other two
pairs uncorrelated. A panel is named by the pair's two parameters:
`bound__drift` is the correlation between drift and boundary.
*Bias* is the mean estimate minus the generating value, 0.4 or 0.
*Share excluding 0* is the
share of replications whose 95 % CrI does not contain zero: for the 0.4
pair, the chance that a study of this size shows the correlation to
differ from zero (its power).

The CrIs of the 0.4 correlation contain it in nine or ten of the ten
replications at every design, but they are
`r fmt(min(target$ci_width))` to `r fmt(max(target$ci_width))` wide, so
they say little about its size. They exclude zero in at most
`r fmt_up(target_max_50, 1)` of the
replications with 50 subjects and
`r fmt_up(max(target$rejection_rate[target$n_subjects == 20]), 1)` with 20,
both at 300 trials: even then, a study with 50 people missed a
correlation of 0.4 between drift and boundary in `r miss_k` of
`r reps` replications (Wilson interval of the miss rate
`r interval(miss_k, reps)`).
With 20 subjects and 30 trials the estimate is pulled towards zero
(`r fmt(pick(target, 20, 30)$mean_estimate)` against an in-sample
`r fmt(pick(target, 20, 30)$in_sample)`, the mean correlation of the
values actually drawn; both are in the table below).

<details>
<summary>The correlation numbers per design</summary>

```{r correlation-table, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  subjects = cors$n_subjects, trials = cors$n_trials,
  pair = pair_label[cors$term], generating = fmt(cors$true_value, 1),
  `in sample` = fmt(cors$in_sample),
  `mean estimate` = fmt(cors$mean_estimate),
  covered = covered(cors$coverage),
  `CrI width` = fmt(cors$ci_width),
  `CrI excludes 0` = fmt(cors$rejection_rate, 1),
  check.names = FALSE
), row.names = FALSE, align = "r")
```

</details>

## How many trials?

Take a threshold for r_low, 0.80 by default, a common convention for
measures used to rank individuals; 0.70 and 0.90 are given for readers
with another threshold. The answer is the smallest number of trials at
which r_low reaches the threshold for every parameter, and stays there
at every larger number of trials in the grid.

One more condition: at that design, the coverage of every population
mean must lie within one MCSE of 0.95, with the MCSE taken at 0.95,
`sqrt(0.95 × 0.05 / 10)` = `r fmt(res$coverage_mcse, 3)`. With ten
replications, 9 or 10 covered intervals out of 10 pass (0.90 is 0.05
from 0.95), and 8 or fewer fail (0.80 is 0.15 from it). Intervals of
exactly the right width pass with probability `r fmt(p_pass, 3)`, so a
design whose `r n_terms` population means all have such intervals fails
the condition with probability `r fmt(1 - p_pass^n_terms)`, if the
`r n_terms` pass independently. A failure is weak evidence that the
intervals are too narrow, but a design at which they are would be a
poor recommendation, however well it ranks people. `smallest_design()`
applies this rule to a grid summary:

```{r readoff-code, eval = FALSE}
s <- summary(out)
smallest_design(
  s[s$level %in% c("subject", "population"), ],
  c(r_low = 0.8),
  coverage_check = TRUE
)
```

It answers per parameter. The table below gives, for each number of
subjects and threshold, the largest answer over the three parameters,
the one that holds for every parameter. The column *using r* applies the
threshold to r instead of r_low, without the coverage condition; the
script computes it itself, because `smallest_design()` does not take r
as a target. Where
it is smaller, either r meets the threshold but ten replications are too
few to be sure that it does, or the coverage condition moved the answer
up.

```{r readoff, echo = FALSE}
in_grid <- function(x) ifelse(is.na(x), "not reached in this grid", x)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  subjects = readoff$n_subjects, bar = fmt(readoff$threshold, 2),
  `smallest number of trials` = in_grid(readoff$smallest_with_coverage),
  `using r` = in_grid(readoff$smallest_point),
  check.names = FALSE
), row.names = FALSE, align = "r")
```

With 50 subjects and bmm `r bmm_version`, a study needs
**`r smallest(50, 0.8)` trials** per person for an r_low of at least
0.80 on every parameter. The grid has nothing between its trial counts,
so "300" means more than 100 and at most 300. The answers in this
section hold at the generating values of this study, chiefly drift's
between-subject SD of `r res$sds[["drift"]]` on the link scale: r and
the reliability compare how much people differ with how precisely each
is estimated, so where people differ more or less, the answer can
change. `drift` decides the r_low
part of each answer: at 100 trials its r_low is
`r fmt(pick(subj, 50, 100, "drift")$r_low)`, at 300
`r fmt(pick(subj, 50, 300, "drift")$r_low)`. That is also why 0.90 is
not reached: drift's r at 300 trials,
`r fmt(pick(subj, 50, 300, "drift")$r, 6)`, meets it only in the sixth
decimal (the 300 under *using r*), and its r_low does not. The
0.80 answer is safe on
r_low but not on coverage: `bound` covered in
`r covered(pick(pop, 50, 300, "bound")$coverage)` replications at that
design, and one more miss would turn the answer into "not reached in
this grid".

The answer at 0.70 shows how much ten replications can decide. By r_low
alone it is `r smallest(50, 0.7, "smallest")` trials. But at that
design `bound` covered in
`r covered(pick(pop, 50, 100, "bound")$coverage)`, so the rule moves on
to `r smallest(50, 0.7)` trials. With one more covered interval the
answer would have been `r smallest(50, 0.7, "smallest")`, and the
second run of this script (see "The run"), with different starting
values, gave exactly that. Read it as "100 or 300".

The number of subjects does not change the r_low part of these
answers: by r_low alone, 20 subjects need
`r smallest(20, 0.7, "smallest")` trials at 0.70 and
`r smallest(20, 0.8, "smallest")` at 0.80, as 50 do. More people
narrow the interval of r and of the population estimates; they do not
measure each person detectably better.
At the 0.80 threshold, r alone would say 100 trials with 20 subjects: drift's
r there is `r fmt(pick(subj, 20, 100, "drift")$r)`, but its r_low is
`r fmt(pick(subj, 20, 100, "drift")$r_low)`.

## Reproducing the study

[`vignettes/articles/precompute/recovery-ezdm.R`](`r script_url`) runs
the grid and writes the results this page reads, to
`vignettes/articles/assets/recovery-ezdm.rds`. It needs bmm
`r bmm_version` or later, brms, cmdstanr and CmdStan, and a copy of the
bmmtools source. Run it from the package's root folder with
`Rscript vignettes/articles/precompute/recovery-ezdm.R`; it took
`r fmt(res$minutes, 0)` minutes for the run shown here, four chains in
parallel. The
fitted models go to `vignettes/articles/precompute/fits/`.
